'''''Asphodelus aestivus''''', the '''summer asphodel''', is a species of [[Asphodelus|asphodel]], a common Western Mediterranean [[geophyte]] with a short vertical rhizome and basal leaves. Its flowers are [[actinomorphic]], pinkish-white, with six perianth segments, 14–19 mm long and six stamens of the same length, in two whorls. Its distribution is limited to the Western Mediterranean, mainly found in [[Portugal]] and [[Spain]] on the European mainland.<ref name="EURO_MED_ASP_AEST">{{citation |title=''The Euro+Med PlantBase''|work=[[the information resource for Euro-Mediterranean plant diversity]] |publisher=[[Botanic Garden and Botanical Museum Berlin-Dahlem]] |url=http://ww2.bgbm.org/EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=9024&PTRefFk=8000000 |access-date=2018-03-04}}</ref><ref name="Plants_World_ASP_AEST">{{citation |title=''Plants of the World Online''|work=[[the reference for global plant names]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:531446-1 |access-date=2020-08-11}}</ref> There has been a lot of confusion over the nomenclature and taxonomy of the species, owing to its similarity to ''[[Asphodelus ramosus]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lifante |first1=Zoila Díaz |last2=Valdés |first2=Benito |title=Lectotypification of Asphodelus ramosus (Asphodelaceae), a Misunderstood Linnaean Name |journal=Taxon |date=1994 |volume=43 |issue=2 |pages=247–251 |doi=10.2307/1222883 |jstor=1222883}}</ref><ref name="VPG">{{citation |title=''Vascular plants of Greece: an annotated checklist''|work=[[Englera 31]] |publisher=[[Botanic Garden and Botanical Museum Berlin-Dahlem]] |url=http://portal.cybertaxonomy.org/flora-greece/intro |access-date=2018-03-04}}</ref> It grows in dry grasslands, phrygana and on rocky or sandy ground.<ref name="iucn status 20 November 2021" />

==Physical characteristics==
The ''Asphodelus aestivus'' is a [[geophyte]], having an underground storage organ which enables the plant to survive adverse conditions, such as excessive heat and drought. Its leaves, growing to a height of {{convert|60|cm}}–{{convert|80|cm}}, contain alkaloids that are harmful to sheep and goats in the wet, winter months, but during the summer when their leaves dry out, they lose their toxicity.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Rhizopoulou |first=S. |title=Ecophysiological Adaptations of Asphodelus aestivus to Mediterranean Climate Periodicity: Water Relations and Energetic Status |journal=Ecography |volume=20 |issue=6 |pages=626–633 |jstor=3683251 |date=1997 |doi=10.1111/j.1600-0587.1997.tb00431.x}}</ref><ref name="Avi Shmida 2005, p. 77">Avi Shmida, ''MAPA's Dictionary of Plants and Flowers in Israel'', Tel-Aviv 2005, s.v. ''Asphodelus aestivus'' (p. 77) {{ISBN|965-521-017-0}} (Hebrew)</ref>
In the [[Iberian Peninsula]] it flowers from June to September, although in the [[Algarve]] (SW Portugal) it may flower in May or at the end of April. There,  the leaves are already withered by the time the plants flower.<ref>See p.  177 in: {{cite journal |last=Díaz Lifante |first=Zoila |title=Reproductive biology of Asphodelus aestivus (Asphodelaceae) |journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution |volume=200|issue=3/4 |pages=177–191 |jstor=23642889 |date=1996 |doi=10.1007/bf00984934|s2cid=189878402 }}</ref>

==Uses==
Some traditional folk usages of the plant (could refer to several species of Asphodelus) have been to make a glue from the plant's root. ''Serish'' is the name for the adhesive made from the root and used in Persian & Iranian papermaking and bookbinding, in particular as a surface size and to laminate paper together for the boards of Persian lacquer bindings.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bainbridge |first=Abigail |title=Conservation of Books |publisher=Routledge |year=2023 |isbn=978-0-367-75490-7 |location=London |language=English}}</ref> A remedy against warts is also derived from its root.<ref name="Avi Shmida 2005, p. 77"/> According to [[Dioscorides]], a concoction made from its roots (mixed with wine) induces vomiting.<ref>Dioscorides, ''[[De Materia Medica]]'' (Book II, § 199).</ref> Formerly, the entire plant was used in treating poisonous snake bites (its efficacy yet to be proven scientifically).
